Oamenii de știință avertizează că topirea ghețarilor, reducerea stratului de zăpadă și încălzirea solului permanent înghețat amenință echilibrul climatic, resursele de apă dulce și siguranța zonelor de coastă, potrivit unui studiu publicat în revista Science.

medical.title: Personalized pharmacy care reduces knee arthritis impairment and treatment costs, trial finds
medical.summary: A personalized, community-based intervention for people with knee osteoarthritis improved outcomes and saved money for most participants, a new study has shown. Te Tauwhiro Turi mā te Rongoā | Knee Care for Arthritis through Pharmacy Service (KneeCAPS), run by the University of Otago, Wellington—Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka, Pōneke, trialed the effectiveness of providing evidence-based information and access to care through community pharmacies for people with knee osteoarthritis.

medical.title: Two brain regions use the same information to shape choices differently
medical.summary: The human brain, like that of other mammals, is organized into different areas with distinct functions. While specific experiences or stimuli can activate several brain regions at once, different areas often use or process this information for different purposes.

medical.title: Mouse study reveals how zinc shortages may disrupt gut health
medical.summary: A new Cornell study suggests that even a mild, chronic shortage of zinc can quietly rewire the intestinal tract, and that the small intestine and the colon respond in strikingly different ways.

medical.title: Not getting enough sleep? Here's how it's affecting your memory
medical.summary: Have you recently walked into a room and forgotten why you went there? Or found yourself reading the same email three times because nothing seems to stick? Perhaps you've struggled to remember the name of a friend of a friend.

medical.title: Uneven access to cancer surgeons is linked to higher digestive cancer mortality
medical.summary: Nearly half of U.S. counties have no surgeon who performs gastrointestinal or hepatopancreatobiliary (liver, pancreas, gallbladder and bile ducts) cancer operations, and residents of those counties have higher death rates from several of those cancers even after accounting for socioeconomic factors and rurality, according to a study published in the Journal of the American College of Surgeons.

medical.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
medical.summary: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

medical.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

medical.title: A converted shipping container became an unexpected source of mental health help in South Africa
medical.summary: Sisanda Hani enters a former shipping container at a community center in South Africa, slips off her shoes and plunges into a sea of blue plastic balls. The 40-year-old mother of a teenager with ADHD and epilepsy lets the balls envelop her and screams.

medical.title: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis
medical.summary: A groundbreaking study reveals that acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive blood cancer, can begin developing more than 50 years before diagnosis, with the first cancer-driving mutation appearing before age 20 in two-thirds of cases. Scientists discovered that these mutated cells grow in surprisingly predictable patterns, accelerating dramatically as additional mutations accumulate.

medical.title: How you know your hand belongs to you: Brain mapping reveals three stages
medical.summary: The feeling that your hand belongs to your body arises from a complex interplay among brain regions that become active in a specific sequence, beginning even before your hand is touched. This was demonstrated in a study from Karolinska Institutet, in which researchers mapped participants' brain activity millisecond by millisecond. The results may, in the long term, contribute to a better understanding of disturbances in body perception after a stroke.

medical.title: Number of U.S. adults living with stroke projected to double to nearly 20 million by 2050
medical.summary: Nearly 20 million U.S. adults are projected to be living with stroke by 2050, almost twice as many as today, with the steepest increases among adults younger than 45 and among Asian and Hispanic adults, according to a new scientific statement published in Stroke. The annual economic burden of stroke is also projected to increase—more than fivefold—reaching nearly $423 billion.

medical.title: Air pollution exposure linked to faster spinal bone loss
medical.summary: Higher recent exposure to air pollution from traffic and other sources is associated with slightly faster bone loss in the spine among older adults in metropolitan areas, according to a large new study being presented next week at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA).

medical.title: Researchers find teens are more likely to use tobacco, alcohol and marijuana when adults at home smoke or vape
medical.summary: Researchers from Children's Hospital of Philadelphia found that adolescents whose parents, caregivers or other adults at home use tobacco or e-cigarettes were substantially more likely to use tobacco, alcohol, marijuana and other substances and to screen positive for high-risk substance use. Rates were highest when both the parent and another adult in the home used these products. The findings were published in the journal Pediatrics.

medical.title: Daily cannabis use surpasses daily drinking among Canadians under 50, survey finds
medical.summary: Six years after cannabis legalization, more adults under 50 in Canada use cannabis daily than drink every day, and daily cannabis smoking is now as common as daily cigarette smoking for adults under age 35, according to new research in CMAJ (Canadian Medical Association Journal) .

medical.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.

medical.title: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue
medical.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising hidden function of a protein that may hold the key to repairing damaged muscles and treating muscular dystrophy. Known for protecting chromosomes, TRF2 also helps muscle stem cells maintain their identity and regenerate injured tissue. When scientists removed the protein in mice, muscles struggled to repair themselves, and muscular dystrophy progressed dramatically faster.

medical.title: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide
medical.summary: A surprising new study suggests that where men get their protein may be linked to their testosterone levels. Researchers studying more than 2,500 men found that higher animal protein intake, particularly from dairy, was associated with lower testosterone, while plant protein was linked to higher levels. The findings raise intriguing questions about how everyday food choices might relate to male hormone levels.

medical.title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
medical.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.

medical.title: Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why
medical.summary: Colorectal cancer is making an alarming comeback in the United States after more than 20 years of declining rates, and the increase is no longer limited to younger adults. A major new study found rising rates across nearly every age group under 70, including older Americans who have historically benefited most from cancer screening.

medical.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
medical.summary: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.

science.title: TED talks and podcasts with slower shifts between ideas tend to be more popular
science.summary: Do you dream of going viral? New research by SFI program postdoctoral fellow Shuhao Fu and linguists at Zhejiang University could offer the insights you need.

science.title: How is Gen Z changing what we eat? These writers found out by asking over 20,000 young people
science.summary: How will we eat in 2050? Will AI-generated, personalized nutrition programs suggest we eat edible insects and drink a glass of synthetic milk for dinner?

science.title: Reduce, resharpen, reuse: Ancient stone tools reveal a regional pattern in southwest China
science.summary: The value of a stone tool can long outlast its first sharp edge. Across 27 locations in southwest China, archaeologists have found evidence of a toolmaking approach that preserved enough stone to allow repeated sharpening—and sometimes the same piece was used as both a tool and a source of fresh flakes for new cutting edges.

science.title: A trick marketers use to sell you things can also persuade rats to enter traps
science.summary: Have you ever wondered why restaurants include outrageously expensive bottles of wine on their menus?

science.title: New toolkit enhances mineral sands understanding
science.summary: Researchers from Curtin University's Timescales of Mineral Systems Group at the Curtin Frontier Institute for Geoscience Solutions (CFIGS) have developed a suite of analytical tools to improve understanding of Australia's heavy mineral deposits, paving the way for more efficient mineral sands exploration.

science.title: How to use small, everyday moments to strengthen family connections
science.summary: In the whirlwind of work demands and family obligations—including planning vacations and holiday celebrations—many parents assume they need to go all out and spend lots of money to build family bonds.

science.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
science.summary: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

science.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
science.summary: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

science.title: Kuala Lumpur otters raise river revival hopes
science.summary: Beneath a tangle of highways in the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur, a family of otters rolls around in a patch of riverside sand, delighting the few passersby who notice them.

science.title: Hidden for 100 million years: X-rays reveal an ancient flower from the age of dinosaurs
science.summary: In a new paper published in the American Journal of Botany, a team of scientists from the U.S. and UK reveal an incredible fossil from the mid-Cretaceous period (around 100 million years ago), opening up a new window into the early evolutionary history of modern-day plants.

science.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
science.summary: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

science.title: Laser Focus at the Top of the World
science.summary: A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.

science.title: Robot submarine exploring world's deepest ocean trench finds unprecedented volcanic activity
science.summary: Fifty-two million years ago, the Pacific tectonic plate began to slide under the Philippine Sea plate, forming the Mariana Trench, the deepest known valley on the Earth's ocean floor. The deepest part of this abyss, the Challenger Deep, is almost 11,000 meters (36,000 feet) below sea level. But why is it so deep? Scientists trying to answer this question sent a remotely operated vehicle to collect samples around the Deep, where they found evidence of the world's deepest underwater explosive volcanic eruptions.

science.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
science.summary: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

environment.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.

environment.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
environment.summary: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

environment.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
environment.summary: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.

environment.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
environment.summary: A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.

environment.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.summary: In the whirlwind of work demands and family obligations—including planning vacations and holiday celebrations—many parents assume they need to go all out and spend lots of money to build family bonds.

mix_items.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
mix_items.summary: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

mix_items.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
mix_items.summary: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

mix_items.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

mix_items.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

mix_items.title: A converted shipping container became an unexpected source of mental health help in South Africa
mix_items.summary: Sisanda Hani enters a former shipping container at a community center in South Africa, slips off her shoes and plunges into a sea of blue plastic balls. The 40-year-old mother of a teenager with ADHD and epilepsy lets the balls envelop her and screams.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis
mix_items.summary: A groundbreaking study reveals that acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive blood cancer, can begin developing more than 50 years before diagnosis, with the first cancer-driving mutation appearing before age 20 in two-thirds of cases. Scientists discovered that these mutated cells grow in surprisingly predictable patterns, accelerating dramatically as additional mutations accumulate.

mix_items.title: Kuala Lumpur otters raise river revival hopes
mix_items.summary: Beneath a tangle of highways in the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur, a family of otters rolls around in a patch of riverside sand, delighting the few passersby who notice them.

mix_items.title: How you know your hand belongs to you: Brain mapping reveals three stages
mix_items.summary: The feeling that your hand belongs to your body arises from a complex interplay among brain regions that become active in a specific sequence, beginning even before your hand is touched. This was demonstrated in a study from Karolinska Institutet, in which researchers mapped participants' brain activity millisecond by millisecond. The results may, in the long term, contribute to a better understanding of disturbances in body perception after a stroke.

mix_items.title: Number of U.S. adults living with stroke projected to double to nearly 20 million by 2050
mix_items.summary: Nearly 20 million U.S. adults are projected to be living with stroke by 2050, almost twice as many as today, with the steepest increases among adults younger than 45 and among Asian and Hispanic adults, according to a new scientific statement published in Stroke. The annual economic burden of stroke is also projected to increase—more than fivefold—reaching nearly $423 billion.

mix_items.title: Air pollution exposure linked to faster spinal bone loss
mix_items.summary: Higher recent exposure to air pollution from traffic and other sources is associated with slightly faster bone loss in the spine among older adults in metropolitan areas, according to a large new study being presented next week at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA).

mix_items.title: Hidden for 100 million years: X-rays reveal an ancient flower from the age of dinosaurs
mix_items.summary: In a new paper published in the American Journal of Botany, a team of scientists from the U.S. and UK reveal an incredible fossil from the mid-Cretaceous period (around 100 million years ago), opening up a new window into the early evolutionary history of modern-day plants.

mix_items.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
mix_items.summary: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

mix_items.title: Researchers find teens are more likely to use tobacco, alcohol and marijuana when adults at home smoke or vape
mix_items.summary: Researchers from Children's Hospital of Philadelphia found that adolescents whose parents, caregivers or other adults at home use tobacco or e-cigarettes were substantially more likely to use tobacco, alcohol, marijuana and other substances and to screen positive for high-risk substance use. Rates were highest when both the parent and another adult in the home used these products. The findings were published in the journal Pediatrics.

mix_items.title: Daily cannabis use surpasses daily drinking among Canadians under 50, survey finds
mix_items.summary: Six years after cannabis legalization, more adults under 50 in Canada use cannabis daily than drink every day, and daily cannabis smoking is now as common as daily cigarette smoking for adults under age 35, according to new research in CMAJ (Canadian Medical Association Journal) .

mix_items.title: Laser Focus at the Top of the World
mix_items.summary: A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.

mix_items.title: Robot submarine exploring world's deepest ocean trench finds unprecedented volcanic activity
mix_items.summary: Fifty-two million years ago, the Pacific tectonic plate began to slide under the Philippine Sea plate, forming the Mariana Trench, the deepest known valley on the Earth's ocean floor. The deepest part of this abyss, the Challenger Deep, is almost 11,000 meters (36,000 feet) below sea level. But why is it so deep? Scientists trying to answer this question sent a remotely operated vehicle to collect samples around the Deep, where they found evidence of the world's deepest underwater explosive volcanic eruptions.

mix_items.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
mix_items.summary: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

mix_items.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.

mix_items.title: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue
mix_items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising hidden function of a protein that may hold the key to repairing damaged muscles and treating muscular dystrophy. Known for protecting chromosomes, TRF2 also helps muscle stem cells maintain their identity and regenerate injured tissue. When scientists removed the protein in mice, muscles struggled to repair themselves, and muscular dystrophy progressed dramatically faster.

mix_items.title: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that where men get their protein may be linked to their testosterone levels. Researchers studying more than 2,500 men found that higher animal protein intake, particularly from dairy, was associated with lower testosterone, while plant protein was linked to higher levels. The findings raise intriguing questions about how everyday food choices might relate to male hormone levels.

mix_items.title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
mix_items.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.

mix_items.title: Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why
mix_items.summary: Colorectal cancer is making an alarming comeback in the United States after more than 20 years of declining rates, and the increase is no longer limited to younger adults. A major new study found rising rates across nearly every age group under 70, including older Americans who have historically benefited most from cancer screening.

mix_items.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.

mix_items.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.

mix_items.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
mix_items.summary: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
mix_items.summary: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.

mix_items.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
mix_items.summary: A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.

mix_items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.
